mainEntity.name: Why do we divide by n − 1 for a sample?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the deviations are measured from the sample mean rather than the unknown true mean, the raw sum of squares runs low. Dividing by n − 1 (Bessel's correction) makes the sample variance an unbiased estimate of the population variance.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between standard deviation and standard error?

acceptedAnswer.text: Standard deviation describes the spread of individual values. Standard error of the mean, s ÷ √n, describes how much the sample mean itself would vary from sample to sample, so it shrinks as the sample grows while the standard deviation does not.

mainEntity.name: How much do outliers affect standard deviation?

acceptedAnswer.text: A great deal, because deviations are squared. One extreme value can inflate the standard deviation substantially. If outliers are a concern, compare it with the interquartile range, which is far less sensitive.

mainEntity.name: Should I choose sample or population?

acceptedAnswer.text: Choose population only if your list contains every member of the group you are describing. If it is a sample used to learn about a larger group, choose sample. When in doubt, sample is the standard choice.

mainEntity.name: What does the coefficient of variation tell me?

acceptedAnswer.text: It expresses the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean, so you can compare the relative spread of data measured on different scales. It is only meaningful when the mean is not close to zero and the data is on a ratio scale.
